questions.stem: A platform team ships an enterprise managed policy that denies `Bash(curl:*)`. A developer adds an allow rule for `Bash(curl:*)` to their project `.claude/settings.json`, and also passes `--allowedTools "Bash(curl:*)"` on the command line. What happens when Claude Code attempts a curl command?

options.text: The command runs, because the CLI flag has the highest precedence.
The command runs, because project settings override enterprise policy for project-scoped work.
The command is denied, because enterprise managed policy sits above every other settings source.
Claude Code prompts the user, because the conflicting rules cancel each other out.

questions.explanation: Settings resolution runs highest-to-lowest: enterprise managed policy → command-line arguments → `.claude/settings.local.json` → `.claude/settings.json` → `~/.claude/settings.json`. Managed policy exists precisely so that a developer cannot re-enable something the organisation has forbidden, so neither the project allow rule nor the CLI flag can lift the deny.

distractor_notes.A: CLI flags beat project and user settings, but they sit *below* managed policy.
distractor_notes.B: Inverted. Project settings are near the bottom of the chain, not the top.
distractor_notes.D: There is no cancellation semantic; the highest-precedence source simply wins.

analogy.text: A Service Control Policy at the AWS Organizations level behaves the same way: an account-level IAM policy that says `Allow s3:*` cannot grant what the SCP denies. Managed settings are Claude Code's SCP.

questions.stem: A nightly job must ask Claude Code to summarise the day's commits and write the result to a file, with no terminal attached. Which invocation is correct?

options.text: `claude "summarise today's commits" > summary.md`
`claude -p "summarise today's commits" > summary.md`
`claude --resume "summarise today's commits" > summary.md`
`claude --interactive "summarise today's commits" > summary.md`

questions.explanation: `-p` / `--print` is non-interactive (headless) mode: Claude Code runs the prompt to completion, prints the final result to stdout and exits. That is the only form safe for cron, CI runners and any context without a TTY.

distractor_notes.A: Without `-p` the CLI starts an interactive REPL, which will hang or misbehave with no TTY.
distractor_notes.C: `--resume` reopens a previous session and still expects interaction unless combined with `-p`.
distractor_notes.D: There is no `--interactive` flag; interactive is the default.

analogy.text: This is the same distinction as `psql` vs `psql -c "SELECT 1"`, or `vim` vs `sed`. Pipelines need the one-shot form that exits with a status code.

snippet.title: Headless summary job
snippet.code:
claude -p "Summarise today's commits for the release notes" \
  --output-format json \
  --allowedTools "Bash(git log:*)","Read" \
  > summary.json

questions.stem: An engineer closed their terminal mid-refactor. They want to reopen the exact same conversation, including the file context Claude had already read, without being shown a picker. Which command should they run from the same directory?

options.text: `claude --continue`
`claude --resume`
`claude /clear`
`claude --restore-context`

questions.explanation: `--continue` (`-c`) immediately reopens the most recent conversation for the current directory. `--resume` (`-r`) shows an interactive list of past sessions to pick from — useful, but it is a picker unless you pass a specific session ID.

distractor_notes.B: Correct family, wrong ergonomics: `--resume` prompts with a session list.
distractor_notes.C: `/clear` wipes conversation history — the opposite of the goal.

analogy.text: `--continue` is `tmux attach` (grab the last session); `--resume` is `tmux ls` followed by `tmux attach -t <name>`.

questions.stem: A team is authoring a custom slash command `/deploy-check` that should be available to everyone who clones the repository and should be restricted to read-only git inspection. Select the TWO correct implementation facts.

options.text: The file belongs at `.claude/commands/deploy-check.md` and is committed to the repository.
The file belongs at `~/.claude/commands/deploy-check.md` so it survives repository changes.
Tool restriction is expressed with an `allowed-tools` key in the command's YAML frontmatter.
Tool restriction requires a separate `PreToolUse` hook; slash commands cannot scope tools.
The command must be registered in `settings.json` under a `commands` array before it is visible.

questions.explanation: Project commands live in `.claude/commands/` and are shared through version control; personal commands live in `~/.claude/commands/`. A command's markdown file carries YAML frontmatter, where `allowed-tools` narrows what the command may invoke. Discovery is filesystem-based — no registration step.

distractor_notes.B: That is the personal scope; it would not reach teammates who clone the repo.
distractor_notes.D: Hooks are a valid extra layer, but frontmatter already scopes tools.
distractor_notes.E: Commands are discovered from the directory; there is no registry array.

analogy.text: `.claude/commands/` is to a team what a committed `Makefile` target is: everyone who clones gets it. `~/.claude/commands/` is a shell alias in your own dotfiles — invisible to the rest of the team.

snippet.title: .claude/commands/deploy-check.md
snippet.code:
---
description: Verify the branch is safe to deploy
argument-hint: [environment]
allowed-tools: Bash(git status:*), Bash(git log:*), Read
---

Check whether HEAD is safe to deploy to $1.
Report: unpushed commits, dirty files, and any TODO markers touched since the last tag.

questions.stem: During a long session a developer notices responses degrading and the context indicator near its limit. They want to keep working on the same task while reclaiming context. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Run `/clear`, then re-explain the task from scratch.
Run `/compact` with a focus instruction so the conversation is summarised but task continuity is preserved.
Restart the terminal so a fresh process allocates a larger context window.
Switch to a smaller model, which increases the available context window.

questions.explanation: `/compact` replaces the transcript with a summary while retaining the thread of work, and it accepts an instruction (`/compact focus on the migration plan and the failing tests`) so you control what survives. `/clear` is the right tool only when you are genuinely switching tasks.

distractor_notes.A: Correct only at a task boundary; here it throws away work in progress.
distractor_notes.C: The window is a model property, not a process property.
distractor_notes.D: Model choice does not enlarge the window in the way implied, and a smaller model would not help reasoning quality here.

analogy.text: `/compact` is `VACUUM` — reclaim space, keep the data. `/clear` is `TRUNCATE` — fast, empty, and everything is gone.

questions.stem: Which permission mode lets Claude Code apply file edits without prompting, while still asking before it runs shell commands?

options.text: `plan`
`acceptEdits`
`bypassPermissions`
`default`

questions.explanation: `acceptEdits` auto-approves file edit tools for the session while leaving other tool classes — notably Bash — under the normal prompting rules. `plan` forbids mutation entirely, `bypassPermissions` skips all prompts, and `default` prompts on first use of each tool.

distractor_notes.A: Plan mode is read-only: no edits at all.
distractor_notes.C: Bypasses everything including Bash — far broader than asked.

analogy.text: `acceptEdits` is a stage with automatic transition for artefact updates but a manual-approval action still gated in front of the deploy step.

questions.stem: A CI job needs to fail the build when Claude Code's headless run reports an error, and it must parse the token cost from the same invocation. Which `--output-format` should be used?

options.text: `text` — then grep stdout for the word ERROR.
`json` — a single structured result object including cost and an error flag.
`markdown` — rendered tables are easy for downstream tools to read.
`yaml` — the only format that includes usage metadata.

questions.explanation: `--output-format json` emits one machine-readable result object carrying the final text, session id, duration, usage/cost fields and an `is_error` indicator. `stream-json` is the incremental variant when you need events as they happen. Grepping free text is exactly the brittleness structured output exists to remove.

distractor_notes.A: Works until a commit message contains the word ERROR.

analogy.text: Same reason a CodeBuild buildspec writes a `reports` JSON artefact instead of asking the pipeline to scrape CloudWatch log text: contract over scraping.

snippet.title: Gate a pipeline on structured output
snippet.code:
result=$(claude -p "$PROMPT" --output-format json)
if [ "$(echo "$result" | jq -r '.is_error')" = "true" ]; then
  echo "$result" | jq -r '.result' >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "$result" | jq -r '.total_cost_usd'

questions.stem: A monorepo developer starts Claude Code in `services/api/` but needs it to also read a shared schema package at `../../packages/schema`. What is the correct way to grant that access?

options.text: Symlink the package into the current directory.
Use `/add-dir ../../packages/schema`, or start with `--add-dir`.
Set `bypassPermissions` mode, which removes directory scoping.
Copy the package into `services/api/vendor/`.

questions.explanation: Claude Code scopes filesystem access to the working directory. `/add-dir` (in-session) and `--add-dir` (at launch) add extra roots, and `permissions.additionalDirectories` in settings makes it durable for the whole team.

distractor_notes.A: Symlink games obscure the dependency and still may not be traversed.
distractor_notes.C: Permission mode governs prompting, not the directory allow-list.
distractor_notes.D: Duplicating source is a maintenance regression, not an access solution.

questions.stem: Which statement about Claude Code surfaces is correct?

options.text: The IDE extension is a separate product with its own model and settings store.
The CLI, IDE extensions and desktop app are surfaces over the same agent, sharing settings and `CLAUDE.md`.
Custom slash commands only work in the CLI, never in the IDE extension.
MCP servers configured in `.mcp.json` are CLI-only and ignored by other surfaces.

questions.explanation: The surfaces differ in presentation, not in engine. The same settings hierarchy, memory files, subagents, skills, hooks and MCP configuration apply, which is why a `.claude/` directory committed to a repo works for every teammate regardless of how they launch Claude Code.

distractor_notes.A: Shared configuration is the whole design point.
distractor_notes.D: Project-scoped MCP config is read by every surface.

questions.stem: An architect wants every session in one repository to default to a specific model, without each developer typing `/model`. Which approach is correct and team-shareable?

options.text: Add a `model` key to the project's `.claude/settings.json` and commit it.
Add `export ANTHROPIC_MODEL=...` to each developer's `.zshrc`.
Put the model name in `CLAUDE.md` and ask Claude to honour it.
There is no way to pin a model per repository.

questions.explanation: `settings.json` carries a `model` key and is committed with the repository, so the default applies to everyone who works there. Environment variables work but are per-machine; `CLAUDE.md` is instruction text, not configuration, and cannot change which model is serving the session.

distractor_notes.B: Works, but is per-developer and drifts.
distractor_notes.C: A model cannot switch the model it is running on by reading a document.

questions.stem: You are standardising Claude Code across 400 engineers. Select the THREE controls that belong in enterprise managed settings rather than in project settings.

options.text: A deny rule preventing reads of `**/.env` and `**/credentials.json`.
The list of MCP servers a particular microservice needs.
Forcing traffic through Amazon Bedrock rather than the public API.
Disabling `bypassPermissions` mode organisation-wide.
The repository's build and test commands.

questions.explanation: Managed settings are for controls that must not be overridable by an individual: secret-file deny rules, the inference endpoint (compliance and data residency), and removing escape hatches such as `bypassPermissions`. Per-repository facts — which MCP servers a service uses, how it builds and tests — belong in project settings and `CLAUDE.md`, where teams own them.

distractor_notes.B: Service-specific and legitimately per-repo; belongs in `.mcp.json`.
distractor_notes.E: Project knowledge, not policy; belongs in `CLAUDE.md`.

analogy.text: Managed settings are cluster-scoped admission policy (Gatekeeper / Pod Security Admission). Project settings are the namespace's own Deployment spec. You do not put a service's replica count in cluster policy, and you do not let a namespace opt out of the security baseline.

questions.stem: A developer reports that Claude Code 'cannot see' an MCP server that works for a colleague. Which single command gives the fastest authoritative view of installed servers and their connection state?

options.text: `/doctor`
`/mcp`
`/status`
`/context`

questions.explanation: `/mcp` lists configured MCP servers with their scope and connection status, and is where you authenticate remote servers. `/doctor` checks the installation health generally, `/status` reports account and session state, `/context` visualises context-window usage.

distractor_notes.A: Broader install diagnostics; will not enumerate server connection state.

questions.stem: A slash command file contains the line `Review PR $1 against the standards in $2.` The user runs `/review-pr 482 docs/standards.md`. What is substituted?

options.text: `$1` becomes `482 docs/standards.md` and `$2` is empty.
`$1` becomes `482` and `$2` becomes `docs/standards.md`.
Nothing is substituted; only `$ARGUMENTS` is supported.
The command errors because positional parameters require a `params` frontmatter key.

questions.explanation: Custom commands support both `$ARGUMENTS` (the whole argument string) and positional `$1`, `$2`, … for individual tokens. Positional parameters let one command take structured input without parsing it yourself.

snippet.title: .claude/commands/review-pr.md
snippet.code:
---
description: Review a pull request against a standards document
argument-hint: [pr-number] [standards-file]
allowed-tools: Bash(gh pr view:*), Bash(gh pr diff:*), Read
---

Review PR $1 against the standards in $2.
List blocking issues first, then advisory notes.

questions.stem: A regulated bank needs Claude Code to run for 2,000 engineers with no source code leaving their AWS account boundary, central spend attribution per team, and no per-developer API keys. Which configuration best meets all three requirements?

options.text: Each developer sets `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from a shared vault entry.
Enterprise managed settings set `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1`, engineers authenticate with existing IAM roles, and spend is attributed through AWS cost allocation tags.
Developers run Claude Code locally with telemetry disabled to prevent any egress.
A single shared service account runs Claude Code on a bastion host that engineers SSH into.

questions.explanation: Bedrock keeps inference inside the customer's AWS account and region, IAM roles remove the need to distribute long-lived keys, and AWS cost allocation gives per-team attribution. Enforcing it through managed settings means a developer cannot quietly point back at the public API.

distractor_notes.A: A shared key defeats attribution and is a credential-sprawl risk.
distractor_notes.C: Disabling telemetry hides usage from you; it does not change where inference happens.
distractor_notes.D: A shared bastion identity destroys attribution and creates a single high-value target.

analogy.text: Same pattern as replacing hard-coded access keys in EC2 apps with an instance profile: identity comes from the platform, the data path stays inside the account, and Cost Explorer can slice spend by tag.
